rv.q: In just over a year, three new UK productions of the opera have gone political: the Royal Opera at the start of last season, Glyndebourne and now English National Opera. Each has offered an individual slant, though it has to be said at the outset that ENO’s is by far the least convincing of the three.

Vocally, this is a disappointing evening, with neither Chaz'men Williams-Ali's Cavaradossi, nor Christopher Purves' Scarpia able to summon either the lyrical richness required by the opera's doomed hero on the one hand, nor the dark, malignant snarl of opera's smooth, satanic supervillain on the other.
This is not, I'm afraid, a vintage Tosca – but Purves's Scarpia just might be.
This take on a timeless tale about love, power and sacrifice feels fresh and resonant: it could be situated in the Balkans in the 1980s or even in Ukraine right now.

Christopher Purves has a rather more meaty presence as the villainous Scarpia, the police chief and would-be lover of Tosca. He struts about in uniform, directs his goons to track down the state’s enemies and conducts summary executions.

Tosca is made of sturdier stuff, especially with Ben Glassberg in the pit conducting the ENO Orchestra on superlative form: the pounding, passionate score emerges as the unchallenged victor of the evening.
Annilese Miskimmon's new staging is the sixth I've encountered at the Coliseum, and easily the worst.
Miskimmon's Tosca is an enjoyable and accessible production, complete with spectacular (unspoiled) 'shocks', excellent performances and modern commentary.
The standout performance comes from the ENO orchestra under Ben Glassberg, who embody every ounce of the majesty of Puccini's score.

cn.t: ENO's contemporary Tosca proves a misconceived production with uneven casting that fails to deliver dramatic impact, though Glassberg's conducting and occasional moments of urgency provide some redemption.
